lesson_title: The Pap Pot Rule: Why Volcanoes Ooze or Explode
hook_text: Every cook already knows why some volcanoes explode. It's the pap pot rule.
clip_script: Stand at the stove with two pots. In the first, a thin vegetable soup simmers: bubbles rise through it easily and pop softly at the top — blip, blip — nothing dramatic. In the second, a stiff pap thickens: the bubbles cannot slip through that heavy porridge, so steam gathers under the surface until it bursts free with that angry PLOP that spits scalding blobs at your wrist. Every cook knows which pot to fear. You now understand volcanoes. In thin, runny magma, the gas bubbles out gently, so the volcano never builds pressure: it oozes. Rivers of glowing lava pour out and cool into wide gentle slopes. In thick, stiff magma, the gas is trapped exactly as in the pap pot — worse, because the stiff melt plugs the pipe like a cork in a bottle. Pressure stacks up for years, sometimes centuries, and when the plug fails the mountain does not leak; it detonates. What decides thick or thin? Mostly silica — and that traces back to the plates: pulling apart gives runny basalt, diving under gives the thick, dangerous brew. The geography chooses the pot.
visual_style: Split screen of a softly simmering soup and a spitting pap pot, morphing into a gentle shield volcano and an exploding composite cone; a cork straining in a bottle neck as pressure gauges climb.
mood: Kitchen danger — familiar stove-top physics scaled up to a mountain.
pacing: Calm on the soup, tightening on the pap pot, detonating at the plug failure, cool landing on 'the geography chooses the pot'.
